opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a common mental model where safety decisions are made by some executive in a room, and researchers either have a seat at that table or they don't. In my experience, that's not really how it works. A lot of what actually shapes outcomes is much more diffuse and much more mundane.

One of the biggest levers technical researchers have is simply making safety *legible and cheap*. If you can turn a vague concern like "this model might be deceptive in some contexts" into a concrete eval, a dashboard, or a technique that slots into an existing pipeline, it becomes dramatically easier for a decision-maker to act on it. Decision-makers at these companies are juggling a huge number of competing priorities, and the things that get done are disproportionately the things that are well-scoped, have clear evidence behind them, and don't require someone to take a massive leap of faith. So a lot of influence comes from doing the unglamorous work of translating safety ideas into something actionable.

The second thing is credibility, which compounds over time. If you're someone who's done genuinely good technical work, who's been right about things, who's reasonable and doesn't cry wolf about everything, then when you *do* raise a concern, people listen. Some safety-minded people, myself included at times, are tempted to treat everything as a crisis. That can burn credibility pretty fast. Being calibrated, saying "I think this one actually matters, and here's why," is a much stronger position.

Third, relationships matter a lot. Knowing the people on the product teams, the people who run training, the people doing policy, means you hear about decisions before they're locked in. A lot of influence is about being in the loop early, when changing course is cheap, rather than objecting at the end when everything's already committed.

I'd also say it's worth being honest about the limits. A technical researcher is not going to single-handedly override strong commercial or competitive pressures. Sometimes the right model is less "I will steer the company" and more "I'll make sure that when key decisions happen, the best possible tools and evidence exist, and the people deciding have heard a well-reasoned safety perspective." That sounds more modest, but I think it's actually where a lot of the marginal value is.

And finally, there's a real role in simply being a person inside the organization who cares and is paying attention. Culture is made up of individuals, and having a critical mass of people who take these risks seriously, who'll ask "have we actually tested for this?" in a meeting, does shift norms over time, even if no single instance looks dramatic.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making safety work actionable and building relationships, but does not identify supporting senior internal safety advocates through technical research.

r002.rationale: It says a technique that fits an existing pipeline makes it easier for decision-makers to act, but does not state that the technique is already implemented or that this makes its adoption easier to approve.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a question I've thought about a lot, because it's basically my job. And my honest answer is that the single biggest lever a technical researcher has is not writing a persuasive memo. It's being the person who actually understands the thing.

Let me unpack that. When a frontier lab is making a hard call — do we ship this model, do we need an extra round of evals, is this behaviour we saw in red-teaming a real concern or an artefact — the people making that decision are usually smart, busy, and not experts in the specific technical question. They're going to defer to whoever in the room has the most credible, legible understanding of what's actually going on. If you've spent six months staring at the model's internals, or you've built the eval that surfaced the issue, you have a kind of authority that no amount of eloquence can substitute for. People listen to you because you can say "here's the plot, here's what happens when we ablate this, here's why I think the simple explanation is wrong," and they can't easily argue with it.

So I think step one is just: do genuinely good, careful work on questions that matter for decisions, and make sure the results are communicated in a way a decision-maker can actually use. A lot of researchers underrate the second half. A 40-page paper is not a decision input. A clear one-page summary with the key uncertainty flagged is.

Step two, which I think people also underrate, is relationships and trust built over time. You influence decisions by being the person people come to before the decision is made, not the person who complains afterwards. That means being reliably calibrated — if you cry wolf on everything, you get tuned out very fast. If you say "I think this is fine" when it's fine, and "I think this is actually scary" when it's scary, people start to update on you. I've seen researchers lose a lot of influence by being maximally alarmed about everything, even when they were right on some of it.

The third thing is picking your battles and being pragmatic about what the company can actually do. There's a failure mode where someone comes in with "we should pause all development" and is ignored, versus "here's a specific test we could run in the next two weeks that would tell us whether this specific concern is real" and gets a yes. The second one is less satisfying but it moves the world more. Incremental wins compound, and they build the credibility that lets you make bigger asks later.

And then the honest caveat: there are limits. There are commercial pressures, there's competition, and a researcher can't override those. I don't want to oversell this. But I think the interface between research and decisions is a lot more porous than people outside labs imagine. The decision-makers mostly do want to get this right, and if you can hand them a crisper picture of reality than they had before, that gets used. Interpretability has been a nice example of this — a few years ago it was a fairly academic field, and now I'm regularly being asked "can you help us understand why the model did this" on things that feed directly into real calls.

So, short version: be technically excellent on decision-relevant questions, be legible and calibrated, build trust before you need it, and ask for things that can actually happen.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can influence decisions through strong, decision-relevant technical work, but does not identify supporting senior internal safety advocates as a way to do so.

r002.rationale: It suggests proposing a specific test that could be run, but does not say that providing an already implemented safety technique makes decision makers more likely to approve its adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to turn a vague concern into something concrete enough that it can change a decision. “This model might be deceptive” is a difficult thing for an organisation to act on. “Here’s a setting where the model reliably misleads the evaluator, here’s what we’ve ruled out, and here’s how we could test whether our mitigation works” gives people something to work with.

And that means understanding the decisions people actually face. Are they deciding whether to deploy a model, how much autonomy to give it, or what monitoring to put in place? What evidence would change their mind? You can do technically excellent research that has very little influence if it doesn’t connect to any of those questions, or if the result arrives after the decision has been made.

For interpretability, I’d want to be quite careful about the strength of the claims. Finding something concerning inside a model could give you a reason to investigate further. Failing to find it doesn’t necessarily establish that the model is safe. Being explicit about that distinction is part of making your work useful and earning trust.

But I also wouldn’t put all the responsibility on individual researchers being persuasive. You want processes where concerning evidence gets documented, reaches the people with authority to act, and can trigger further testing or a pause. Researchers can make those processes much better by supplying good evidence, but the organisation has to be willing to respond to it.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can provide useful evidence and improve organizational processes, but it does not identify supporting senior internal safety advocates as a way to influence decisions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses testing whether a mitigation works, but does not say that offering an already implemented safety technique makes adoption easier for decision makers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most useful things a technical researcher can do is turn a vague concern into something concrete enough that it can change a decision. “This model might be deceptive” is a difficult thing for an organisation to act on. “Here’s a setting where we reliably observe this behaviour, here’s what we think causes it, and here’s a test we can run on the next model” gives people something to work with.

But doing good research isn’t the whole process. You need to understand who actually makes the relevant decision, what evidence they would find compelling, and when they need it. If your result arrives after a deployment decision has effectively been made, it’s much harder for it to matter. So I’d encourage researchers to talk to the people doing evaluations and making deployment decisions early, and ask: what uncertainty could I resolve that would change what you do?

And I think being calibrated is really important. Be clear about what your experiment demonstrates, what you’re extrapolating, and what you don’t know. You want people to trust that when you raise a concern, there’s something substantive behind it. That also means being willing to say when a result is reassuring.

The ambition should be to make safety-relevant questions empirically tractable, and then help get that evidence into the actual decision process. A paper can be part of that, but it isn’t necessarily the endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response recommends engaging evaluators and deployment decision makers, but does not identify supporting senior internal safety advocates through technical research.

r002.rationale: It says concrete evidence can inform decisions, but does not state that providing an already implemented safety technique makes adoption easier to approve.
